analysis|10-04|1912|Συμμαχική διακοίνωση πριν από τον πόλεμο|Allied joint note before the war|In the Balkans, the Christian countries had concluded alliances to confront Ottoman rule, while national claims and minority issues in Macedonia and Thrace were getting sharper. Montenegro was already ready to declare war. The region lived in a climate of tension that rose from year to year. // Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia sent a joint note to the Sublime Porte, asking for reforms in the Christian areas. The note amounted to an ultimatum demanding reforms. The Porte rejected the demands. // The countries withdrew from Constantinople, opening the way to the First Balkan War, which changed the map of the region. This crisis showed that diplomacy could no longer contain the competing ambitions of the Balkan states.

analysis|10-04|1944|Απελευθερώνεται η Πάτρα|Patras is liberated|At the end of 1944 the Germans were leaving Greece, as their position in the Balkans had become untenable after the advance of the Allies and the Soviets. The Peloponnese was gradually abandoned by the occupation forces. The withdrawal was carried out with caution, because the Germans feared resistance during their retreat. // Patras, one of the largest cities of the country, was liberated, and its inhabitants celebrated the end of the occupation. The sense of freedom came together with the need to deal with the damage to the city. // The day of liberation remains important for local history and is honoured with events, and the city began its reconstruction after the difficult years of the war. This reconstruction took place in conditions of scarcity, and the city needed years to regain its momentum.

analysis|10-04|1974|Ο Κωνσταντίνος Καραμανλής ιδρύει τη Νέα Δημοκρατία|Konstantinos Karamanlis founds New Democracy|New Democracy of Konstantinos Karamanlis had been founded shortly before the first free elections after seven years of dictatorship, and Karamanlis had returned from Paris to take up the premiership of the transitional government. The Metapolitefsi opened a new course for democracy. The New Democracy party supported the transition to the parliamentary system. // Karamanlis founded New Democracy, which won the elections of November 1974 and shaped the political scene of the Metapolitefsi. The party became one of the two major poles of Greek politics. Its victory confirmed society's trust in Karamanlis' personality. // The party remains to this day a key player in the political life of the country, and its course has been linked with the major decisions of post-junta Greece, from accession to the European Community to the economic reforms of the 1980s.

analysis|10-04|2009|Εκλογές με νικητή το ΠΑΣΟΚ|Elections won by PASOK|The early elections of 2009 took place in an atmosphere of distrust towards the New Democracy government, which had been weighed down by scandals and by the consequences of the global economic crisis. PASOK promised a change of course under the slogan of social support. Society was ready for change, and the debate about transparency in governance had dominated. // Giorgos Papandreou won by a large margin and became prime minister. Shortly afterwards the real size of the public deficit was revealed, and the new government faced a situation much worse than had been presented. // The country entered the debt crisis and the memoranda, with deep consequences for the economy and society. This experience changed the Greek political scene for the following years, and the issue of managing the debt dominated public discussion.

analysis|10-05|1912|Η Ελλάδα κηρύσσει τον πόλεμο στην Οθωμανική Αυτοκρατορία|Greece declares war on the Ottoman Empire|The Balkan countries had formed a network of alliances, completed by the agreements of Greece with Bulgaria and Serbia in 1912. After the Porte's refusal to accept reforms and the start of hostilities by Montenegro, Greece proceeded to declare war. Allied diplomacy had been carefully organised to confront the Ottoman Empire. // The Greek army advanced quickly through Macedonia, Epirus and the Aegean, and the country almost doubled its territory. The speed of the campaign was the result of coordination and leadership. These victories changed the borders of the Greek state. // The First Balkan War was an important step in the course of the Greek state and led, afterwards, to tensions with Bulgaria. The distribution of the gains from the war was not accepted by everyone, and these issues led to the Second Balkan War.

analysis|10-05|1955|Ο Καραμανλής αναλαμβάνει την κυβέρνηση|Karamanlis takes over the government|Alexandros Papagos, prime minister and leader of the Greek Rally, died in early October 1955. King Paul had to choose a successor, and his choice was not self-evident, as there were older politicians with greater prestige. The question of succession concerned the stability of the government. // He finally entrusted the formation of a government to the younger Minister of Public Works, Konstantinos Karamanlis. This choice was an important step for the political life of the country, and showed that the palace's trust was turning to a new figure. // It was the beginning of a long political course which, until 1963 and, after the Metapolitefsi, until 1980, marked the country with reconstruction works and with the course towards the European Community. This period left deep marks on modern Greece.

analysis|10-06|1825|Λήγει η πρώτη φάση της δεύτερης πολιορκίας του Μεσολογγίου|The first phase of the second siege of Missolonghi ends|In 1825 Kioutachis attacked Missolonghi, which was one of the most important centres of the Revolution in western Central Greece. The inhabitants and the fighters fortified the walls and prepared for a long defence, because the town was the key to control of the region. The siege was part of the wider Ottoman effort to take Central Greece. // The attacks were repulsed and the town held out. This resistance strengthened the morale of the Revolution, but the pressure continued, and later Ibrahim came too, which increased the difficulty of the situation. // The siege ended with the Exodus of 1826, which moved Europe and strengthened the philhellenic movement. The Exodus remains one of the most powerful symbols of Greek resistance, and the image of the town became a point of reference for the sacrifice of the fighters.

analysis|10-06|1910|Ο Βενιζέλος γίνεται πρωθυπουργός|Venizelos becomes prime minister|After the Goudi coup of 1909, Greek political life demanded reforms and new faces. Eleftherios Venizelos, a politician from Crete, was called upon by the military and by public opinion to help renew the state. This call reflected the need to modernise the country. // He became prime minister in 1910 and launched an extensive programme of revision of the Constitution and of modernisation of the army and administration. This programme gave the country new dynamism in politics and in the organisation of the state. // The Balkan Wars that followed enlarged Greece, and Venizelos became the dominant figure of the political life of the era, with many disagreements but also great influence. His political legacy was subsequently linked with the National Schism.

analysis|10-06|1912|Ο στρατός απελευθερώνει την Ελασσόνα|The army liberates Elassona|At the start of the First Balkan War, the Greek army of Thessaly, led by the crown prince Konstantinos, crossed the frontier and advanced towards Macedonia. Elassona was the first place on its path, near the old Ottoman frontier line. The advance aimed to open the road to Thessaloniki. // The entry of the army into Elassona and Deskati gave the Greeks their first territories and strengthened their morale. This success showed the readiness of the army at the start of the campaign. // A few days later the battle of Sarantaporos followed, which opened the road to Thessaloniki. The first advance was decisive for the speed of the campaign and for shaping the strategy of the following months.

analysis|10-06|1923|Οι Σύμμαχοι αποχωρούν από την Κωνσταντινούπολη|The Allies leave Constantinople|After the end of the First World War, Constantinople was under Allied occupation, while Kemal's Turkey had won the war in Anatolia. The Treaty of Lausanne, signed in the summer of 1923, set the new relations. The agreement closed the period of international claims in the area. // After its ratification, the Allied troops left the city and the Turkish government took control. The change left the Greek community of the City in a new and difficult position. // Shortly afterwards Ankara became the capital of the Turkish republic. The event marked definitively the end of the Ottoman period and changed the position of the Greek community of the City, which was gradually reduced.

analysis|10-06|1955|Ο Καραμανλής γίνεται πρωθυπουργός για πρώτη φορά|Karamanlis becomes prime minister for the first time|The death of Papagos left open the question of succession within the Greek Rally camp. King Paul, according to the Constitution, had the power to choose who would form a government, and chose Konstantinos Karamanlis. This choice marked the beginning of a new political era for the party. // Karamanlis later founded the National Radical Union and governed for many years, with an emphasis on public works, industrial development and rapprochement with Europe. ERE became the dominant party of the era. // His first premiership marked the post-war history of Greece, and his personal presence was linked with the stability and reconstruction of the country. The forces of his camp remained in government for a long period.

analysis|10-07|1571|Η ναυμαχία της Ναυπάκτου|The naval battle of Lepanto|The Ottoman Empire had taken Cyprus and threatened the Mediterranean. Venice, Spain and the Papal States formed the Holy League, an allied fleet led by Don Juan of Austria. The alliance was the answer of the West to Ottoman expansion. // The great clash took place in the Gulf of Patras, during which the Christian fleet inflicted a heavy defeat on the Ottomans. The battle remained in history as one of the largest naval clashes of the 16th century. // Despite the victory, the Ottomans quickly rebuilt their fleet and kept Cyprus. Naupaktos remained in Europe's memory as an important victory, and for the Greeks as an event that encouraged hopes of liberation.

analysis|10-07|1820|Το «Σχέδιο Γενικόν» της Φιλικής Εταιρείας|The General Plan of the Philiki Etaireia|The Philiki Etaireia had been founded in Odessa in 1814 with the aim of preparing the national revolution. In 1820 Alexandros Ypsilantis became its leader, and the Philiki had to decide where and how the struggle would begin. That decision was critical for the course of the whole undertaking. // The plan envisaged an uprising in the Peloponnese and in the Danubian Principalities, so that the Ottoman forces would be split. The double direction of the plan aimed to draw the enemy away from its key points. // The Revolution began in 1821 and, despite the difficulties in the Principalities, prevailed in the Peloponnese and Central Greece, leading eventually to the foundation of the Greek state. The plan became a basic point of reference for the organisation of the uprising.

analysis|10-07|1831|Καταδικάζεται ο Γεώργιος Μαυρομιχάλης|Georgios Mavromichalis is sentenced|Ioannis Kapodistrias, the first governor of Greece, was assassinated in Nafplio at the end of September 1831, after tension with the Mavromichalis family of Mani. The perpetrators, Georgios and Konstantinos Mavromichalis, were members of the family. The murder took place in the public life of the new state, at a moment of political tension. // Konstantinos was killed by the crowd and Georgios was tried, sentenced to death and executed. The political life of the state, which had already been tested, found itself in a new trial with the murder of the governor. // The murder threw the country into anarchy and political uncertainty, which ended with the arrival of King Otto, and is considered one of the most tragic events of the first years of the Greek state. The memory of Kapodistrias has since remained linked with the vision of state organisation.

analysis|10-07|1944|Η εξέγερση στο Άουσβιτς|The uprising at Auschwitz|In the Auschwitz-Birkenau camp, groups of prisoners, the Sonderkommando, were forced to work in the gas chambers and in the crematoria. Among them were Greek Jews, mainly from Thessaloniki. They knew that they too would be exterminated, and their life was constantly on the edge. // On 7 October 1944 they rose up and blew up one of the crematoria. The uprising was crushed and most of the participants were killed, as they had very few means against the guards. The attempt was one of the few reactions within the place of extermination itself. // The uprising remained as a symbol of resistance within the most horrific environment of the Holocaust and brings to memory the fate of the Jews of Greece, whose community of Thessaloniki was largely annihilated.

analysis|10-07|2020|Η δίκη της Χρυσής Αυγής|The trial of Golden Dawn|The murder of the musician Pavlos Fyssas in 2013 brought the violence of Golden Dawn to the fore and led to a judicial investigation. The trial began in 2015 and lasted more than five years, with hundreds of hearings and many witnesses. The case was one of the largest trials of the Metapolitefsi in Greece. // The Three-Member Appeals Court ruled that Golden Dawn functioned as a criminal organisation and convicted its leaders. The decision was the result of a long process, with a multitude of evidence. // The decision was considered a milestone for democracy and justice in Greece, as it offered an answer to the phenomenon of far-right violence. The trial highlighted the role of justice against a party that had been elected to Parliament.

analysis|10-08|451|Αρχίζει η Δ΄ Οικουμενική Σύνοδος|The Fourth Ecumenical Council begins|In the 5th century the Church had been in intense dispute over the nature of Christ, after the teachings of Eutyches and the Robber Council of Ephesus. Emperor Marcian convened a new council so that unity could be restored. The intensity of the theological disputes had political dimensions. // At Chalcedon the fathers defined that Christ is one person with two natures, divine and human. This formulation became a basic point of theological agreement for the Orthodox and the Western Church. // The decision became a basic dogma of the Orthodox and Western Churches, but it alienated the anti-Chalcedonian churches of the East, with consequences that last to this day. The issue remained open for centuries in the Christian history of the Middle East.

analysis|10-08|1838|Ο Κολοκοτρώνης μιλάει στην Πνύκα|Kolokotronis speaks at the Pnyx|Theodoros Kolokotronis, a leading figure of the Struggle of 1821, had been imprisoned earlier and now lived in Athens as a respected veteran. University students wanted to hear the words of a man who had lived the Revolution. His presence was a symbol of the generation of the Struggle. // In his speech at the Pnyx he spoke about unity, education and the sacrifice of the fighters. The text of the speech was addressed to the young, who saw in Kolokotronis the living link with the Struggle. // The Exhortations are considered one of the best-known texts of Greek history and are often cited as a legacy to the younger generations. The speech remained in memory as an appeal for unity and for values that go beyond party division.

analysis|10-08|1912|Ο ελληνικός στόλος ελευθερώνει τη Λήμνο|The Greek fleet liberates Lemnos|At the start of the First Balkan War, the Greek navy aimed to secure control of the Aegean and to prevent the Ottoman fleet from leaving the Dardanelles. Lemnos, an island with a strategic position, was a basic target of the operations. Control of the island had direct importance for the naval operation. // The recapture of the island gave the Greek fleet the natural harbour of Moudros, which became a naval base. This base allowed the fleet to operate with greater flexibility in the Aegean. // From there the fleet controlled the exit from the Dardanelles and gained a decisive advantage in the Aegean, which contributed to its later victories. Moudros remained in history as an important naval station.

analysis|10-08|1912|Ξεκινά ο Α΄ Βαλκανικός Πόλεμος|The First Balkan War begins|The Ottoman Empire, weakened after the Italo-Turkish war and internal crises, gave the Balkan countries the opportunity to act. The states of the Balkan League had prepared the war extensively, with agreements that defined the areas of operations. The alliance was the basis of the attack. // Montenegro took the first step, and Serbia, Bulgaria and Greece followed. Within a few months the Ottomans lost most of their European territories, which changed the map of the peninsula. // The victory, however, created disagreements over the division, which soon led to the Second Balkan War. The alliances that had worked against the Porte dissolved, and the former allies found themselves in confrontation.

analysis|10-09|1912|Η μάχη του Σαρανταπόρου|The battle of Sarantaporos|After crossing the frontier, the Greek army of Thessaly, under the crown prince Konstantinos, faced the Ottoman forces in the narrows of Sarantaporos, a strong defensive position on the road to Kozani and Thessaloniki. This position was critical for the course of the campaign. The attack was carried out with careful planning. // The Greeks won and forced the Ottomans to withdraw. The victory gave great self-confidence to the army and opened the road to Macedonia. This success was the first important victory of the land campaign. // After it followed the liberation of Kozani and then the battle of Giannitsa and the entry into Thessaloniki. This sequence of operations completed the great advance of the army into Macedonia.

analysis|10-10|1862|Καταλύεται η μοναρχία του Όθωνα|The monarchy of Otto is overthrown|King Otto had ruled Greece since 1833, but dissatisfaction with his absolutist policy and with the absence of an heir was growing. The revolution broke out in Nafplio and spread quickly to Athens, while the king was touring the Peloponnese. The speed of the uprising showed how cut off the regime was from society. // A provisional government of three men was formed and Otto left the country. The removal of the king opened the way for new developments. // The election of a new king, Georgios I in 1863, followed, and the adoption of a more liberal Constitution in 1864. The transition took place in conditions of broad social participation and expectations.

analysis|10-10|1935|Το κίνημα του Κονδύλη|The Kondylis coup|In the 1930s the Second Hellenic Republic was in instability, with continuous political crises and clashes between the Venizelists and the anti-Venizelists. The political system found it difficult to secure stable governments, and public opinion was tired of the constant changes. These differences had their roots in the National Schism. // General Georgios Kondylis, a former Venizelist, had turned towards the royalists. His change of side was symbolic of the fluidity of the era, when the army and politics were being formed anew. His movement affected the balance of forces. // With the coup the republic was abolished, and after a referendum in November 1935 King George II returned to the throne. A few years later, in 1936, the dictatorship of Metaxas was established, and this period profoundly changed the political course of the country. The change left behind a society with limited freedoms.

analysis|10-10|1941|Το πρώτο διάγγελμα του ΕΑΜ|The first proclamation of EAM|During the Occupation the Greek people faced hunger, oppression and the need to organise resistance. The National Liberation Front was founded in September 1941 on the initiative of the Communist Party and other political groups. Its creation gave an organised form to the resistance of society. // Its first call to the people shaped the political face of the movement and was addressed to broad circles of citizens. Its success was based on the ability to bring together people from different social groups. // EAM became the largest resistance movement in the country, with its military wing, ELAS. Its activity influenced the events of the Occupation and of the post-war period, and its legacy remains the subject of intense historical debate.

analysis|10-10|1993|Το ΠΑΣΟΚ επιστρέφει στην εξουσία|PASOK returns to power|The government of New Democracy of Konstantinos Mitsotakis, which had won in 1990 with a narrow majority, was shaken by internal disputes and the departure of MPs. The inability to maintain its majority led to the need for new elections. The political crisis had reached a point that did not allow the smooth running of government. // Early elections were held in 1993, and PASOK of Andreas Papandreou won with a clear majority and formed his third government. The victory gave the party the opportunity to implement its programme. // Papandreou was in poor health and resigned in 1996, when he was succeeded by Kostas Simitis, while the policy of the period focused on preparing the country for European economic and monetary union. This effort shaped the economic policy of the decade.

analysis|10-11|1912|Η Κοζάνη ελευθερώνεται|Kozani is liberated|After the victory at Sarantaporos, the Ottomans withdrew into the interior of Macedonia, and the road to Kozani, a large city of Western Macedonia, remained open. The Greek army advanced quickly to exploit the victory. The speed of the advance was a key factor of the campaign. // The entry into the city took place with enthusiasm from the Greek population, after centuries of Ottoman rule. The emotion of the inhabitants showed the depth of the desire for liberation. // The liberation of Kozani gave the army a base for further advance towards Veroia and Thessaloniki and strengthened the atmosphere of rapid campaign. The city thus became a stage on the path to Macedonia.

analysis|10-11|1944|Οι Γερμανοί φεύγουν από το Ηράκλειο|The Germans leave Heraklion|In autumn 1944 the military situation of the Germans in the Balkans was worsening, and the occupation forces were gradually withdrawing from many parts of Greece. In Crete the Axis forces gathered in the west of the island. This movement showed that the withdrawal was under way. // The departure from Heraklion gave the city's inhabitants the chance to celebrate the end of the occupation after almost three and a half years. The relief of the inhabitants was great, while uncertainty about the future remained. // German forces remained in other parts of the island, and Crete had suffered greatly, especially from reprisals and the harsh treatment of the population. The liberation of Heraklion thus became part of a gradual process.

analysis|10-11|1998|Οι πρώτες δημοτικές εκλογές με τον νόμο Καποδίστρια|The first municipal elections under the Kapodistrias law|The reform of local government, called Kapodistrias, merged hundreds of small communities and municipalities into larger ones, with the aim of being able to provide better services and carry out larger projects. The small scale of the municipalities had become an obstacle to modern needs. The reform was one of the biggest changes in local administration. // In the elections of 1998 citizens voted for the first time for the new councils of the merged municipalities. The institution changed the map of local government, and the new structure brought changes to the relationship between citizens and local institutions. // Later new reforms followed, such as the Kallikratis reform of 2010, which continued the same course of consolidation. This path showed that the question of local government remained at the centre of political debate.

analysis|10-12|1862|Ο Όθων φεύγει οριστικά από την Ελλάδα|Otto leaves Greece for good|The revolution of October 1862 began in Nafplio and succeeded quickly, as the government had no significant support. King Otto and Queen Amalia, who were returning from a tour of the Peloponnese, were unable to return to Athens. This situation shows how easily his authority collapsed. // They boarded a British ship and left the country for ever. Their departure closed the era of the Bavarian monarchy, and the decision of the British side facilitated the transition. // Greece entered a period of searching for a new king, and subsequently George I of the House of Glücksburg was elected. This election opened a new page in the political history of the state.

analysis|10-12|1944|Απελευθερώνεται η Αθήνα από τα γερμανικά στρατεύματα|Athens is liberated from the German troops|In 1944 the course of the war changed, and Germany had to withdraw its forces from the Balkans. Athens, which had suffered from the hunger of the winter of 1941-42 and from reprisals, was preparing for the departure of the conquerors. The city waited anxiously for the end of the occupation. // The Germans left the city and the Athenians celebrated in the streets. The joy of the inhabitants was accompanied by concern about the political developments. // A few weeks later the government of national unity returned, but the political differences between EAM and the government soon led to the Dekemvriana and to the great crisis of the civil war. This period opened a new cycle of conflict.

analysis|10-12|1953|Συμφωνία για τις αμερικανικές βάσεις|Agreement on the American bases|After the Civil War and Greece's accession to NATO in 1952, the United States was the main ally and protector of the country. The Cold War confrontation between West and East made Greece's strategic position very important. The alliance shaped foreign policy for decades. // The agreement regulated the presence of American installations and forces in the country. These bases formed part of the defence architecture of the West. // The issue of the bases became a subject of political dispute for decades, especially after the junta and the events of Cyprus, and remains a point of discussion about Greek-American relations. The debate returns at every critical moment for the two countries.

analysis|10-14|1912|Ο ελληνικός στρατός περνά τα στενά του Βερμίου|The Greek army crosses the Vermion pass|After the capture of Kozani, the Greek army continued towards Veroia and Thessaloniki. On the way lay the rugged narrows of Vermion, where the Ottomans could organise a defence. The geography of the area made every step of the campaign demanding. // The Greeks crossed the narrows and continued the advance, while the Ottoman forces failed to stop the campaign. The crossing was one more step in the rapid march towards Macedonia and showed the army's ability to move over difficult terrain. // The crossing contributed to the liberation of Veroia and Edessa a few days later. This success strengthened the army's self-confidence and was linked with the next victories of the campaign.

analysis|10-14|1944|Ο Ιερός Λόχος φτάνει στην ελεύθερη Αθήνα|The Sacred Band arrives in liberated Athens|The Sacred Band was a special forces unit of the Greek army of the Middle East, which had fought alongside the British. After the withdrawal of the Germans from Athens, the first Greek units returned to the capital. The unit had gained a reputation for its operations in the war. // Their arrival was symbolic, because it showed the return of the legitimate Greek government and army. Their presence on the streets of the capital gave a sense of normality to society. // The welcome by the people was warm, but the political tension between EAM and the government already created concern about the future of the country. This tension would remain as a heavy legacy of the era.

analysis|10-15|1837|Ιδρύεται η Σχολή Καλών Τεχνών της Αθήνας|The School of Fine Arts of Athens is founded|The School of Fine Arts of Athens was created within the needs of the newly founded Greek state. The state needed craftsmen, architects and engineers to build the capital and the public infrastructure. So a school was founded where technical and artistic subjects were taught, initially as a section of the School of Arts. // Over the years the institution grew and was split into several schools. This development reflected the broadening of higher education in the country. // From it emerged the National Technical University of Athens, one of the most important higher education institutions in the country, and the School of Fine Arts, which continues the artistic tradition. This dual heritage links the technology and the art of the country.

analysis|10-16|1909|Το κίνημα των κατώτερων αξιωματικών του Ναυτικού|The revolt of the junior naval officers|A few weeks after the Goudi coup of August 1909, the dissatisfaction that existed in the army spread to the navy. Officers demanded reforms, promotions on meritocratic criteria and the modernisation of the fleet. This situation showed the need for renewal of the armed forces. // Konstantinos Typaldos led the movement at Piraeus, and the government retreated on several demands. The government's stance showed the pressure the officers exerted on political life. // The movement strengthened the climate of renewal that led to the rise of Venizelos and to the reorganisation of the armed forces, before the Balkan Wars. The navy thus gained new strength for the next operations.

analysis|10-17|1864|Ψηφίζεται το Σύνταγμα του 1864|The Constitution of 1864 is voted|After the expulsion of Otto and the arrival of George I, the country needed a new Constitution that would regulate the relations between the throne and the people. The National Assembly worked in 1863-64 and voted a text more democratic than the previous ones. This process was substantial for the new political order. // It established the crowned democracy, with one chamber and universal male suffrage. This institutional arrangement gave society a framework of participation that had not existed before. // It remained in force, with revision, until 1911, and contributed to the political development of the country and to institutional stability in the 19th century. The Constitution remained a point of reference for the Greek constitutional tradition.

analysis|10-17|1915|Η Βρετανία προσφέρει την Κύπρο στην Ελλάδα|Britain offers Cyprus to Greece|In autumn 1915 Serbia faced the danger of an attack by Austro-German and Bulgarian forces. Britain, in order to persuade Greece to help Serbia, proposed the cession of Cyprus, which it had administered since 1878. The proposal was connected with the general diplomacy of the war. // Prime Minister Venizelos was in favour of participation in the war, but King Konstantinos wanted neutrality and the proposal was rejected. This dispute showed how divided the Greek leadership was. // This clash deepened the National Schism, while Cyprus remained under British sovereignty for decades, until independence in 1960. The 1915 proposal thus remained as a missed opportunity for the Greek question.

analysis|10-18|1827|Ο Φαβιέρος ελευθερώνει τη Χίο|Fabvier liberates Chios|The French philhellene Charles Fabvier, an experienced officer, organised a regular army and landed on Chios, which had been devastated in 1822 by the Ottoman massacres. The effort to liberate it remained a goal of the Revolution. His presence shows the importance of the philhellenes in the struggle. // Fabvier and his men occupied a large part of Chios, but the fortress remained in Ottoman hands and the campaign was not long-lived. This outcome showed the limits of the campaign. // The venture showed the role of the philhellenes and the difficulties that the Revolution faced in the islands of the Aegean. The experience remains in history as one of the first examples of cooperation with foreign volunteers.

analysis|10-18|1912|Απελευθερώνεται η Έδεσσα|Edessa is liberated|In the First Balkan War, after the victory at Sarantaporos and the liberation of Kozani and Veroia, the Greek army continued its advance towards Macedonia, and Edessa was among the targets. The area had strategic importance for the road to Thessaloniki. The advance followed a clear plan. // The town, known for its waterfalls, was liberated, and on the same day Alexandreia also fell. The simultaneous capture of the two towns showed the rhythm of the campaign. // These actions secured control of the area and prepared the battle of Giannitsa, which opened the road to Thessaloniki. Edessa thus became a stage on the path to Macedonia.

analysis|10-18|1918|Γεννιέται ο Κωνσταντίνος Μητσοτάκης|Konstantinos Mitsotakis is born|Konstantinos Mitsotakis was born in Chania, in a family with a political tradition, as his grandfather was a close collaborator of Venizelos. He studied law and entered politics after the war. His family tradition influenced his political choices. // He served as minister in various governments, opposed the junta and went into exile abroad.
